entry.title: Phil Eaton Surveys Memory Management in 40 Major C Projects
entry.content:
Links: theconsensus.dev | lobsters | hacker news

Phil Eaton surveyed 40 major C software projects to examine how they handle memory allocation, finding that only eight projects rely exclusively on manual malloc and free operations. The analysis reveals that while manual memory management remains widespread, many prominent codebases incorporate higher-level primitives such as memory regions, reference counting, garbage collection, and scope-based cleanup compiler extensions.

Memory strategies vary significantly across infrastructure projects, with some prioritizing strict manual control while others lean heavily on specialized allocators. For example, SQLite relies entirely on manual allocation for correctness, whereas projects like Linux and QEMU have increasingly adopted compiler extensions for automated scope cleanup, and others utilize region-based or garbage-collected allocation models.

entry.title: Steinar H. Gunderson Solves the Ancient Norse Fox Board Game
entry.content:
Links: blog.sesse.net | lobsters

Software engineer Steinar H. Gunderson has completely solved the ancient Norse asymmetric board game known as the Fox Game or halatafl, determining that sheep win with perfect play under standard rules. Using a compact bitboard representation, combinatorial number systems, and parallelized state propagation across 64 cores, Gunderson analyzed over two trillion possible board states over a 36-hour run.

The implementation required approximately 1,000 lines of code with no external dependencies, leveraging symmetry optimizations to manage memory and reduce the search space. Gunderson found that sheep maintain a forced win even when reduced to 19 or 18 pieces, while 11 sheep suffice against a single fox, conclusively settling a question left open by previous AI analyses.

entry.title: Daniel Stenberg Marks 30 Years of Internet Transfers With Curl
entry.content:
Links: daniel.haxx.se | lobsters | hacker news

Daniel Stenberg reflects on the 30-year history of curl, which began on November 11, 1996, when Brazilian student Rafael Sagula published a basic HTTP download tool called httpget. Stenberg took over maintenance of the software, expanded its protocol support, renamed it to cURL, and introduced libcurl in 2000 to allow other programs to handle internet transfers.

Over the decades, curl has evolved from a hobby project powering an IRC currency bot into a cornerstone of global internet infrastructure, running in an estimated 30 billion installations. Stenberg attributes the project's longevity to continuous code refactoring, strict backward compatibility, and an independent open-source model.

entry.title: Google DeepMind Uses AI Tool AlphaProof Code to Formally Verify Signal Protocol
entry.content:

Google DeepMind researchers have used a new agentic AI framework called AlphaProof Code to formally verify key cryptographic guarantees of the Signal messaging protocol. Conducted as a four-week proof-of-concept project, the evaluation independently validated the encryption used across major communication platforms like Signal, Google Messages, and WhatsApp without discovering any new vulnerabilities.

While the tool successfully identified known vulnerabilities in older protocol versions, researchers and industry experts emphasize that scaling AI-driven formal verification to entire software codebases remains a significant challenge. DeepMind is releasing the specifications and proofs developed during the project to support broader cryptographic security efforts, though the commercial viability and costs of the technology are not yet clear.
